The grading is very terrible I think as the final exam takes up 70%, which if you accidentally did badly then your entire courses will result in terrible grading. The final exam is also the most ridiculous and terrible part of the course, it requires you to WRITE PYTHON CODING ON A PAPER, but not a computer. Usual coding we try and error in the computer to get the final working code. But how can I check my code if I write it on a paper??? And who as a normal person will write python coding on a paper except for this exam??? So ridiculous.

And the exam is also far more difficult then labs or those lecture notes. Even if you understood all the basics you may still struggle with the exam. And writing the codes on a paper makes it even more challenging as you won’t be able to check whether a code works. A paper won’t tell you if a code works but only a computer will.

The weekly quiz is MCQ based on pre-lecture videos and easy to get full mark with help of AI. Lab submissions is quite straightforward codings and the TA will announce the answers in the middle of the lab if you have focused.

I got full marks in both weekly quiz and lab submission, final exam not announced.

sections.teaching:
Xu Hong actually taught us pretty well. She was passionate about teaching us basic python stuff and always asked us questions and played “games”, trying to make python more interesting to learn. Most of the time no one answered but she kept her passion for the half semester. Her teaching was detailed and she explained different topics step by step. Her notes aka Jupyter Notebook were clean and you would feel like you could really learn a programming language.

Chris in tutorials was pretty good too (subtle foreshadowing), his slides recapped things that were taught in lectures so if you are not attending lectures, you can catch up on tutorials. Participation was needed in tutorials so you have to attend at least 5 (I think?) lectures to get all participation points. He was saying that the finals would be easy and we somehow trusted him. It was definitely not what I expected.
sections.grading: The finals which was held in mid October, was pretty hard. Although I wasn’t in my best shape exam-wise, I wasn’t expecting the difference between weekly exercises (which I will talk about in workload section) and the actual exam. Especially when they gave you a few empty lines for you to code the way they wanted, my brain just shut down at that moment and forgot all if statements and for loops. That part was by far the hardest part. Free coding part was not as bad but there was still pressure on me after completing the fixed coding part and time was running out. The exam was designed to be unexpected so that they could differentiate who is good and who is worse. I had been attending both lectures and tutorials, completing weekly exercises and gaining parti. Finals score wasn’t published but I got a B+. My conclusion would be do the best you can at weekly assignments and attending tutorials. This way you can still fall into B range (I hope) even if you don’t think you do good in the exam.
sections.workload: Weekly exercises are like assignments for the lectures and it was pretty easy. You just have to watch the videos (if you are a master at python, don’t watch at all), to finish the assignments. In tutorials, there weren’t any work except attending. However, if you plan to skip tutorials and still got the attendance (=parti), you can complete something call lab attendance waiver. The waiver is actually the content in the next tutorial and see if you can complete the challenges in the Jupyter Notebook for next chapter. If you have done it, you should submit the notebook on canvas first, then you can show it to the TAs at class. After checking, if they are satisfied with your work, you can leave and saved more than an hour of your life. I had done it several times and it was a pretty good policy. It is optional though so if you’re a master, you should do it, otherwise you can stay at the class and listen to Chris explain topics to you.

4 Weekly Quizzes          20% (5% each)
4 Lab Activities              20% (5% each)
Individual Assignment   10% (up to 5% bonus on top)
Final Exam                     50%

Weekly Quizzes
15 MCs each to check your concepts. Be careful and check your answers before submitting as the scores aren't released until after the deadline, and most people get full marks.

Lab Activities
Write a few lines of code to fulfil the task requirements. They are formatted to guide you to completion, so most people also get full marks.

Individual Assignment
It's like a longer version of the lab activities, with several tasks for you to solve. They give you 2 weeks complete it, and I took ~5 hrs to finish (including lots of checking and refining) and submitted it on day 3. You may want to spread the workload into several days if that's less exhausting for you.
I was never told how the bonus is given, but I guess coding with efficiency and creativity is key.

Final Exam
90 mins to finish 30 MCs, 3 SQs, 2 LQs.
A cheat sheet including almost everything taught in the course is provided, so you only have to understand how it works but not memorize things (which is great for me).
MCs are similar to but somewhat harder than the weekly quizzes.
SQs require you to fill in the blanks in some given codes or ask you about the outputs of the code, basically testing whether you can understand the codes given.
LQs ask you to write code for the tasks. I finished with 15-20 lines of code, so it's not very long, but I suggest checking your own codes several times (if you have time) to search for bugs as it's a PAPER EXAM and you can't rely on the computers.
The paper is longer than I expected. There's sufficient time to finish it for sure, but you can't spend too much time thinking. I actually made quite some mistakes initially, so checking really helps. If you want to spare more time for checking your answers, try responding to the questions instinctively, so practice beforehand is crucial (although I didn't do much).
